narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on your first attempt, and unfortunately, the model predicted a 99.2% probability that you would not pass — a very high level of concern that led to your application being rejected. This does not mean you are incapable of succeeding, but it does signal that your current academic profile differs significantly from students who have gone on to pass the bar exam, and understanding those gaps is the first step toward changing that outcome.

To help explain this decision, the model was tested against ten "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile where certain factors were adjusted just enough to flip the prediction from "will fail" to "will pass." These counterfactual scenarios are not predictions about your future, but rather a map of what the model considers most critical in distinguishing students who pass from those who don't.

What stands out most strikingly from this analysis is that across all ten alternative scenarios, only one factor ever changed: your undergraduate GPA. Every single counterfactual scenario that would have resulted in an approved application involved a shift in your undergraduate GPA, and no other factor — not your LSAT score, not your law school grades, not your enrollment status, not your family income — changed in any of them. This makes undergraduate GPA the single most decisive factor in your case, at least in terms of what the model identified as the tipping point.

The average change in undergraduate GPA across these scenarios was a decrease of 0.1 points, which may seem counterintuitive — a lower GPA leading to a better outcome. However, this reflects a complex pattern the model has learned from historical data, and it should not be interpreted as advice to perform worse academically. Rather, it highlights that your current GPA of 2.90 sits in a particularly sensitive region of the model's decision boundary, and that your overall profile is being evaluated holistically.

To put your situation in broader context, students who passed the bar exam had an average undergraduate GPA of 3.24, compared to your 2.90 — a meaningful gap of about 0.34 points. Similarly, your LSAT score of 34 falls below the average of 37.27 among students who passed, and your law school grades in both your first and third years place you in the 2nd decile of your class, whereas passing students averaged around the 6th decile. These are substantial differences that collectively paint a picture of academic performance that the model associates strongly with bar exam difficulty.

On a more encouraging note, your profile does share some characteristics with successful students: you are enrolled full-time, which aligns with 93.2% of students who passed, and your upper-middle family income background is the most common income bracket among students who passed (45.1%). These factors are working in your favor and were not flagged as areas needing change in any of the counterfactual scenarios.

The most actionable takeaway from this analysis is that strengthening your academic performance — particularly your undergraduate GPA and law school class standing — would have the greatest impact on how your application is evaluated in the future. While your undergraduate GPA is a record of the past and cannot be changed retroactively, focusing intensively on improving your law school grades going forward, and investing in structured LSAT preparation to raise your score closer to the 37–38 range, could meaningfully shift your predicted outcome. The model's message is clear: academic performance is the cornerstone of this decision, and even incremental improvements in that area could make a significant difference in your path toward bar exam success.
